    Instructor Notes

    These notes are for instructors and helpers. They cover preparation, teaching, timing, checkpoints, feedback, the data and the answer keys. The design record (objectives, report card, assessment map, misconceptions and concept map) is on the Lesson Design page. In the Instructor View, the instructor notes from every episode follow these notes, in episode order.

    The Lesson in One Paragraph

    The lesson makes three passes over one nine-step workflow (data, model, fit, check the fit, estimates, check the model, random effect, compare, forecast). In the first pass you demonstrate on Stellako sockeye salmon. In the second, learners repeat each step on Upper Pitt River in the “Your Turn” challenges, and fill in one row of a model report card per episode. In the third, the Capstone, pairs apply the whole workflow to a stock they choose, or to their own data. The Quick Start runs all nine steps in one hour, and each later episode opens one step as one or more recipe cards. Learners copy each recipe into their own my-recipes.R; the finished recipe box (cookbook.R) holds every recipe, in lesson order.

    Before the Workshop

    • Send the Setup page a week ahead, and ask learners to reply (by email or a form) with the line Your setup works. that the setup check prints.

    • Collect the answers to the three self-check questions on the Setup page. Anyone who gets two of the three wrong should take an introductory R lesson first; tell them before the workshop, kindly.

    • Prepare:

      • sticky notes in two colours that colour-blind learners can tell apart: green for “done” and pink for “I need help” (avoid red and orange, which many colour-blind people cannot tell from green); learners also write a question mark on a help note, so that colour is not the only cue;
      • a shared notes document with a “parking lot” section for questions that a later episode answers;
      • a shared table for the capstone share-out, with the columns listed in the capstone (stock; best by AIC, with the AIC difference to the next; best by hindcast skill; random-walk 80% coverage; do AIC and the hindcast agree?; one sentence);
      • printed copies of the Recipe Index;
      • the link to the code handout (files/code-handout.R on the built site), which holds every recipe chunk.

    • Offer an optional setup help desk at 08:30 on Day 1.

    • Rehearse on the computer you will teach from. In a project with data/ and files/ set up as on the Setup page, run:

      R 

      source("files/quick-start.R")
check_fit(opt, sdr)
check_fit(opt_walk, sdr_walk)
c(ricker = aic(opt), walk = aic(opt_walk))

      It takes about 3 seconds and must print four TRUE twice, then the two AIC values:

      OUTPUT 

       finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
 finished      flat    curved finite_se
     TRUE      TRUE      TRUE      TRUE
  ricker     walk
198.2570 178.3082

    Teaching

    • Teach by participatory live coding, with a large font and dark text on a light background. Type everything, say each line as you type it, then explain it again.
    • There are three exceptions to typing:
      • learners who fall behind in the Quick Start may paste from the Quick Start script (quick-start.R); the Quick Start is the only episode where learners may paste whole steps;
      • naive_forecast() in Episode 11 is read together, not typed: it comes from source("files/cookbook.R") in the Starting Point, so learners who skipped the Starting Point run that line (or paste the function into my-recipes.R);
      • the capstone uses the capstone template (capstone-template.R).
    • Make the planned mistakes live, and let learners read the output before you explain it:
      • the missing minus sign in front of sum() (Episode 4);
      • the missing random = argument (Episodes 4 and 8);
      • the random-effect vector that is one value too short (Episode 6).
    • Ask “What questions do you have?”, not “Any questions?”. Write deep questions in the parking lot, labelled with the episode that answers them, and come back to them there.
    • Keep to the lesson’s one way per task. If someone asks about another method, say that it exists and point to where the lesson covers it:
      • lm(): the callout “If You Know lm()” in Writing a Model as a Likelihood;
      • Bayesian fitting, REPORT() and formula packages such as glmmTMB: the Going Further page;
      • optim(): nlminb() does the same job, and the lesson uses one optimiser throughout.

    • Exercises take half of the time. Episodes 1 to 11 have 50 challenges (two of them optional) in 330 minutes of teaching: one every 7 minutes on average.
    • All times are first estimates. After you teach, replace teaching: and exercises: at the top of each episode with the times you measured.

    When you fall behind, never speed up: cut whole pieces, and tell learners where the skipped material is. Cut in this order:

    1. Episode 10 (Many Stocks). Tell the pooled-NPGO story in two minutes at the end of Episode 9: across all 19 stocks, the North Pacific Gyre Oscillation (NPGO) index lowers AIC by 16 without shared year effects, but raises it by 0.6 with them.
    2. In Episode 8, demonstrate the self-test instead of having learners type self_test().
    3. Episode 3, Challenge 2 and Episode 5, Challenge 2.
    4. Episode 11, Challenge 3.
    5. Capstone rows 5 and 6.

    Never cut the Quick Start, Episode 4, the core of Episodes 7, 9 and 11, or capstone rows 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9.

    A workshop can stop at two points and still be useful:

    • after Episode 7: one stock is fitted, reported and checked with residuals (lesson objectives 1 to 4, and the residual part of objective 5);
    • after Episode 9: models can also be compared (objectives 1 to 6).

    Responding to Multiple-Choice Answers

    Every wrong option in a multiple-choice challenge comes from a named misconception. Plan your response before you ask:

    • if most learners pick one wrong answer, re-teach the misconception it names, using the evidence in the table below;
    • if answers are spread out, go back to the last point everyone understood;
    • if almost everyone is right, move on.

    In the table, E03.C2 means Episode 3, Challenge 2.

    Misconceptions, the evidence to re-teach with, and where the lesson targets them.
    # Misconception Evidence (from the lesson’s own runs) Targeted by
    M1 Return the log-likelihood, not its negative opt$convergence is 0 with the message “X-convergence (3)”, opt$objective is -Inf, and the checks are TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE E03.C2, E04.C1
    M2 convergence == 0 means the fit is usable the same output E04.C1
    M3 If the optimiser finished on flat ground, the standard errors are fine two parameters that do one job: finished TRUE, flat TRUE, every standard error NaN E04.C2
    M4 Back-transform as exp(estimate) ± 1.96 SE gives 122.2 to 123.3 instead of 73 to 207 thousand for Stellako’s S_max E05.C1
    M5 A confidence band should contain most data points the 95% band holds 24% of the Stellako points E05.C3, E11.C1
    M6 exp() of a log-scale forecast is the mean median 148, mean 199 thousand recruits E11.C2
    M7 random = means “draw random numbers”; an SD at zero means the fit failed Harrison: four checks TRUE, sd_walk 5e-6, AIC exactly 2.00 above the Ricker E06.C1, E06.C4
    M8 Observed-minus-fitted residuals are fine for random-effect models conditional residuals have SD 0.96 and lag-1 correlation -0.17; one-step-ahead residuals have SD 1.00 and -0.10 Episode 7 spoiler and keypoint
    M9 Models fitted to different rows can be compared by AIC the Ricker on 1958-2021 has AIC 177.2 and appears to beat the random walk on 1948-2021 (178.3); on the same rows the walk wins by 17.6 E09.C3
    M10 Lower AIC means better forecasts Upper Pitt River: AIC prefers the random walk by 11.8, but the Ricker’s hindcast errors are slightly smaller (skill 0.78 against 0.82); Chilko and Birkenhead in the capstone (AIC and the hindcast choose different models), and Late Stuart (the lowest-AIC model forecasts no better than the recent-average benchmark) E11.C4, capstone share-out
    M11 Changing dat after a fit is harmless with the raw RTMB calls, dat$S_new <- 150 after fitting silently changed sdreport()’s mu_new from 1.97 to 1.16 Episode 4 spoiler (demonstration)
    M12 A covariate that lowers AIC is robust pooled NPGO: AIC changes by -16.0 without year effects and +0.57 with them E10.C4
    M13 An SD estimated at zero proves there is no variation self-test: 11 of 50 data sets simulated with sd_walk 0.13 gave an estimate of about zero E06.C4 (option c), E08.C6
    M14 obj$simulate() without arguments uses the fitted values it uses the parameters evaluated last Episode 8 caution
    M15 S_max is a carrying capacity (terminology) Episode 5 caution
    M16 AIC can compare a model of log(R/S) with a model of R the two models describe different responses E09.C5

    Feedback

    • Collect minute cards at lunch on both days: one thing that went well, and one question or thing that was unclear.
    • Collect one-up/one-down at the end of each day: each learner says one thing to keep and one thing to change.
    • Open Day 2 by saying what you changed after Day 1’s feedback (5 minutes).
    • Day 2 starts with the Parsons warm-up, Checking a Model with Simulation, Challenge 1: it rebuilds Day 1’s fitting recipe and reminds everyone of random =.

    Data Notes

    • Stellako brood year 2005 (102 thousand spawners, 11.6 thousand recruits) returned mainly in 2009, one of the poorest Fraser River sockeye returns on record. It is real; do not delete it. Episode 7, Challenge 3 asks what to do about it.
    • Upper Pitt River is the “Your Turn” stock because it behaves like Stellako but has two differences worth discussing: NPGO helps, and AIC and the hindcast disagree.
    • Harrison is the only stock with brood year 2022, so its hindcast from 2007 has 16 forecasts instead of 15.
    • Quesnel and Late Stuart have strong four-year cycles and years with under 1 thousand spawners (25 years for Quesnel, 9 for Late Stuart). Every fit still passes all four checks, but under the random walk Quesnel’s S_max (3481 thousand) is far beyond its data.
    • Early Stuart (in 2019 and 2020 only 46 and 15 fish spawned: 0.046 and 0.015 thousand) and Late Shuswap (S_max beyond the data) are left out of the examples on purpose.
    • Cultus, Portage and Scotch Creek have missing years. Every recipe handles them, but they are not on the capstone menu.
    • The data were supplied with the Pacific Salmon Commission RTMB workshop and described there as “not necessarily official numbers”. The lesson uses them to teach methods; nothing in it is management advice. These stocks matter to First Nations and to commercial and recreational fisheries: treat questions about them with care, following the CARE principles for Indigenous data governance.

    Hidden Curriculum to Make Explicit

    Say these out loud when they first come up; experienced R users do them without thinking.

    • Work in a project, and use relative paths such as data/sockeye.csv.
    • Keep code in a script, not in the console, so you can rerun it.
    • Read an error message from the bottom up, then find it on the Troubleshooting page.
    • Call set.seed() before anything that simulates, so the numbers can be reproduced.
    • Save upper-pitt-river.R as you go: each “Your Turn” challenge adds its code and its row comment as soon as it runs, and by Episode 11 the script runs the stock from the data to a tested forecast.
    • Use new object names in your own experiments (ricker_test, not ricker), so you do not overwrite the demonstration objects that later steps use.

    Answer Keys

    • Upper Pitt River: the full solutions are in the “Your Turn” challenges of Episodes 1 to 11. The completed report card is summarised below.
    • Capstone: the answer key for Quesnel, Late Stuart, Chilko, Harrison and Birkenhead is an instructor note in the Capstone, also collected at the bottom of this page in the Instructor View.
    The Upper Pitt River report card (answer key for the “Your Turn” challenges).
    Row Item Upper Pitt River Challenge
    1 Data 1948-2021, 74 years, spawners 2.1 to 74.6 thousand; S_new = 5.3 thousand spawners (average of 2018-2021) E01.C2, E03.C5
    2 Fits usable four checks TRUE for the Ricker, the random walk, Beverton-Holt and Ricker + NPGO E04.C4, E06.C3, E09.C4
    3 Estimates alpha 8.9 recruits per spawner (95% CI 6.5 to 12.1); S_max 20 thousand spawners (15 to 28), inside the observed range E05.C4
    4 Random effect sd_walk 0.33 (0.14 to 0.78): productivity typically changes by about a third from year to year; 10.4 recruits per spawner in 1948, 16.3 in 1965, 4.7 in 1980, 10.9 in 2000, 2.9 in 2021 E06.C3
    5 Residuals Ricker lag-1 0.47 against a limit of 0.23, long waves over time, QQ plot bends below the line at both ends; random walk lag-1 0.13 E07.C2
    6 Simulation observed lag-1 0.58: reached by 0 of 200 Ricker simulations and 62.5% of random-walk simulations; self-test of the walk: 30 of 30 refits pass, no sd_walk at zero E08.C5
    7 Comparison random walk best: 6.2 below Ricker + NPGO, 7.5 below Beverton-Holt, 11.8 below the Ricker; NPGO helps here (b_npgo 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.48) E09.C4
    8 Forecast skill hindcast from 2007: Ricker skill 0.78, bias +0.74, coverage 0.67; random walk skill 0.82, bias 0.00, coverage 0.60; benchmark coverage 0.40. AIC and the hindcast disagree E11.C4
    9 Forecast random walk: median 12 thousand recruits (80% prediction interval 4.4 to 35 thousand) from 5.3 thousand spawners E11.C4

    Building the Lesson

    • Each episode is knitted in a fresh R session. Episodes 1 and 2 load the data themselves, and Episodes 3 to 11 start with a Starting Point chunk that recreates everything they need. The capstone runs no code: its template and solutions are shown, not run.
    • episodes/files/cookbook.R must stay identical to the code taught in the episodes. If you change a recipe, change it in both places, and in every episode that uses it.
    • config.yaml sets fail_on_error: true, so any unplanned error stops the build. Chunks that are meant to fail are marked error=TRUE.
    • No chunk takes more than about 5 seconds. The slowest is the optional profile interval in Episode 10; the 50-simulation self-test in Episode 8 takes about 2 seconds.
    • Run sandpaper::validate_lesson(headings = TRUE) before you commit. The README explains how to build the lesson locally.

    A Private Repository

    • GitHub Pages can serve a site from a private repository only on a paid GitHub plan, and the site may still be public.
    • Until the lesson is ready to share, build it locally and share the site/docs/ folder as a zip file.

    Introduction: Salmon, Spawners and Recruits

    Instructor Note

    Before the first chunk, check that every learner has a project with data/ and files/ folders and three empty scripts: my-recipes.R, stellako.R and upper-pitt-river.R. Show where the code handout is (files/code-handout.R on the lesson website): it collects the recipe code of every episode. Keep this episode to 25 minutes and do not introduce models yet; the Quick Start does that next.


    Instructor Note

    This question takes 3 minutes; ask for answers by a show of fingers (one to four for a to d). If most learners choose (a), type log(0) and log(1) in the console and read both results aloud. If most choose (d), point out that the ratio has no units, while recruits are in thousands of fish. If answers are spread out, go back to the definition of recruits per spawner in “Salmon in One Minute”.


    Instructor Note

    This challenge takes 7 minutes. Watch for learners who overwrite my_stock with Upper Pitt River: the next episode starts from Stellako, so ask them to use the name pitt. Ask for green sticky notes when the plot appears and row 1 is written.


    Quick Start: The Whole Workflow in Nine Steps

    Instructor Note

    Type steps 1 to 5 live, saying each line aloud; for steps 6 to 9, keep typing but explain only what to look for in the output, because later episodes explain every line. This is the only episode where learners who fall behind may paste from files/quick-start.R. Keep to 60 minutes: aim for four TRUE at QS4 by about minute 20, Challenge 2 done by minute 35, and both AIC values at QS8 by minute 45. If you are behind at QS7, type it while learners paste it from files/quick-start.R, explain only what to look for, and take Challenge 5 orally in one minute. Write deep questions on a “parking lot” list, labelled with the episode that answers them (the table at the end of this episode).


    Instructor Note

    Before QS2, check that everyone has dat: length(dat$S) is 74. The most common problem here is a wrong working directory, which stops read.csv(): help the learner open the project, then rerun the chunk.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes here: green when check_fit(opt, sdr) shows four TRUE, the other colour for any error. The most common problem at this point is a typing error in nll_ricker: compare it with files/quick-start.R.


    Instructor Note

    If many learners choose (a), they think a pattern in the residuals means the fit failed: point back to the four TRUE in QS4, and say that the checks test the fit, while residuals test the model. If many choose (c), show the plot again and count the years above zero before 1990. If answers are spread out, go back to what a residual is: how far each year is from what the model expected, given the years before it.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when learners have the two AIC values. Misconception to listen for: “the model with more parameters always wins”. The penalty counts only the fixed parameters (three for the Ricker, four for the random walk), and Episode 9 shows a model with one more parameter that loses.


    Instructor Note

    Ask two or three pairs which forecast they would trust. Listen for “the random walk, because recent productivity is lower” and “the Ricker, because it uses all 74 years”. Say that Episode 11 settles it, and put the question on the parking lot.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for a green sticky note when learners have the four answers. Watch for learners whose QS9 now uses sdr and opt because they edited it in place in Challenge 4: their forecast is the Ricker’s (a median of 37.1 thousand recruits), not the random walk’s. Watch also for anyone who ran plain source() and got no output. Before the break, ask everyone to switch back to Stellako and rerun the script (Episode 3’s Starting Point chunk also recreates the Stellako data).


    Writing a Model as a Likelihood

    Instructor Note

    Draw the three parts on the board before any code: a falling line, a bell on its side at three places along it, and the labels mu, sigma and normal. The surprise-score picture later in this episode is all the theory learners need: do not derive the likelihood. This section takes about 5 minutes.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when obj$fn(obj$par) prints 144.8. The usual problems are a name typed differently in nll_ricker and in start_ricker (R says object '...' not found, with the name it could not find), and a missing getAll() line (the spoiler below shows this error). The three recipes so far take about 15 minutes together.


    Instructor Note

    Misconception to listen for: “the likelihood is the probability that the parameters are right”. Answer: “it scores the data, given the parameters”. If most learners chose B or C in Challenge 1, point at the plot: the score adds up one surprise per point, and a curve far from many points is very surprised by them.


    Instructor Note

    This challenge targets misconception M1 (returning the log-likelihood instead of its negative). If many learners keep the line without the minus sign, go back to the surprise score: the optimiser always looks for the smallest value, and we want the smallest surprise. If you are behind, cut this challenge (third on the list of cuts in the instructor notes) and tell learners that its solution is on the page.


    Instructor Note

    If many learners choose (c), point to log_Smax: S_max is on the log scale although spawners are not. If many choose (d), point to the score line, where dnorm() receives exp(log_sigma), the standard deviation itself. If answers are spread out, go back to the starting values: log_sigma is -0.027 for Stellako, a number that would be impossible as a standard deviation.


    Fitting a Model and Checking the Fit

    Instructor Note

    In a workshop, skip the optional spoilers “How RTMB Gets Exact Slopes” (below) and “Why Restart Once?”; learners can read them later. Show the data-copy spoiler from the page without typing it: it answers misconception M11, that changing dat after a fit is harmless. If your learners rarely write functions, type fit_model() in two passes: first the three calls and a list of obj, opt and sdr, which you run; then the safety steps and the recipe items, naming each one as you add it.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when ricker$checks shows four TRUE. If a learner’s own fit_model() gives an error, rerunning the Starting Point chunk loads the version in cookbook.R; fix their copy at the break. Then ask for a show of hands on the prediction below before you run rbind() (1 minute). Across all 19 stocks, a single nlminb() call already passes every check for these models, so the restart is insurance for larger models and learners’ own data, not a fix for these data.


    Instructor Note

    Make the sign error live: type nll_sign, fit it, and let learners read the output before you explain anything. A mistake made in front of the room is a teaching moment. Then ask the question below and let learners vote. If most choose (a), they think that convergence == 0 means a usable fit (misconception M2): show m_sign$opt$par, ask what S_max would be, and repeat that code 0 only says the optimiser stopped. If answers are spread out, go back to the valley picture and the four checks. The demonstration and the vote take about 5 minutes.


    Instructor Note

    Give learners 5 minutes alone, then 3 minutes to compare answers with a neighbour. If many match A with cause 1 (log = TRUE missing), point at the 79: the number of estimated parameters is the clue that the random effects were not declared. Cause 3 is the hardest to picture; draw the flat-bottomed trough from the figure.


    Instructor Note

    Check that learners named the fit ricker_pitt. Anyone who overwrote ricker should run ricker <- fit_model(nll_ricker, start_ricker(dat), dat) again before Episode 5, which uses the Stellako fit.


    Estimates, Intervals and Derived Quantities

    Instructor Note

    Challenge 1 targets misconception M4 (back-transforming only the estimate). It comes before ci_table() prints any interval, so learners cannot find the answer on the screen. If most learners choose (a), write both calculations on the board and compare 10.5 to 11.1 with 7.9 to 14.7 (for S_max, the same mistake gives 122.2 to 123.3 thousand instead of 73 to 207). If answers are spread out, go back to step 5 of the Quick Start: the interval is made on the log scale, then both ends go through exp().


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when ci_table(ricker) prints (about 15 minutes into the episode, after Challenge 1). Misconception to listen for: “a 95% interval means there is a 95% chance that the true value is inside”. Say “it is a range that, in 95% of repeated studies, would catch the true value”, and move on; do not dwell on it.


    Instructor Note

    Copy nll_ricker in your script, rename it and add the two lines, saying aloud that each derived quantity goes into a copy of the function with a new name, so the original stays unchanged. In Challenge 2, watch for log(alpha): the function has no object called alpha, but ggplot2 has a function alpha(), so R stops with non-numeric argument to mathematical function (sigma gives the same error); inside the function, use the names in par, such as log_alpha. If you are behind, cut Challenge 2 (third on the list of cuts in the instructor notes) and tell learners that its solution is on the page. Then ask a 1-minute question instead: to report S_rep with an interval that stays above zero, which two lines do you add, and what must the new quantity’s name start with? (Answer: compute log_Srep, then ADREPORT(log_Srep); the name starts with log_.)


    Instructor Note

    If you are behind, do not have learners type predict_recruits(): show it, explain it line by line, and let them use the copy in cookbook.R (the Starting Point chunk loads it). They copy it into my-recipes.R at the break.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 3 is the first appearance of misconception M5 (“a confidence band should contain most data points”); come back to it in Episode 11, Challenge 1. If most learners choose (a) or (d), point at sigma in ci_table(ricker): about two years in three lie within a factor of 2.4 of the curve, above or below it, and the band does not include this scatter. If answers are spread out, go back to the plot and ask what the grey band is about: the curve, or the years.


    Random Effects: Productivity That Changes over Time

    Instructor Note

    Stress that a random effect is an estimated distribution, not random numbers: nothing is drawn at random when the model is fitted. Learners who know lme4 think of random effects as grouping factors (one value per site or per person). Say early that a random effect can also be indexed by time, one value per year, and that Episode 10 shows random effects for groups.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 1 targets misconception M7 (“random = means draw random numbers”). If most learners choose (b), say that fitting the same model twice gives the same answer to the last digit: nothing is drawn. If many choose (a), point at ci_table(walk, "random") in the next recipe, which gives every yearly value with an interval. If answers are spread out, go back to the definition: a random effect is a set of related unknown values that come from a distribution.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when the productivity plot appears (about 20 minutes into the episode). Point at the dashed line: the Ricker’s 10.8 is too low for the 1970s and far too high for the 2010s, which is the residual pattern from step 6 of the Quick Start.


    Instructor Note

    Make the mistake in Challenge 2 live: type the three lines with max(dat$year) and let learners read the error before you explain it. The error message does not name the cause, which is why the Troubleshooting page lists it.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 4 targets misconceptions M7 (“an SD at zero means the fit failed”) and M13 (“an SD at zero proves there is no variation”). If most learners choose (a) or (d), go back to the four checks for walk_h and the two equal negative log-likelihoods: the fit worked, and zero is the answer. If many choose (c), say that Episode 8 simulates data with Stellako’s drift, and that 11 of 50 such data sets also give an SD of about zero. If answers are spread out, go back to the recipe’s three checks.


    Checking a Model with Residuals

    Instructor Note

    Open with the contrast: the four checks test the fit, residuals test the model. Learners who know lm() expect residuals to be “observed minus fitted”; say that for random-effect models these are too small and not independent (misconception M8, in the optional spoiler below), and that the lesson uses one kind of residual for every model. This section takes about 3 minutes; do not explain how oneStepPredict() computes the prediction beyond the two bullet points.


    Instructor Note

    Give learners a minute to write down their prediction before you run the random walk’s QQ plot. Many expect the random walk to remove 2005; it cannot, because productivity drifts slowly and 2005 was one sudden poor year. For scale: the lowest of 74 draws from a standard normal distribution is usually about -2.4, and a value as low as -4.2 turns up in about 1 series in 1000.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes after the lag-1 numbers print; this recipe takes about 12 minutes. Type the three checks as three separate chunks and name each check aloud as you go: shape, pattern, independence. Learners can make the change to res_walk in the spawner plot on their own. If learners notice that the random walk’s recent residuals are more spread out (for your information: without 2005, their SD is 0.78 before 1990 and 1.11 after 2000), say that a change in spread is also a pattern; every model in this lesson keeps sigma constant, so note it as a caveat in row 5 or row 10.


    Instructor Note

    If many learners choose (b), point at the QQ plot (shape) and the lag-1 number (independence) side by side, and say that each check answers a different question. If many choose (c), point back to the TRUE values in the Starting Point output: the fit worked, and residuals test the model, not the fit. If answers are spread out, go back to the pattern plot: the long runs above and below zero are what the lag-1 number measures.


    Instructor Note

    For your information only, not for the learners: Shapiro-Wilk p-values for the Stellako residuals are 0.0009 (Ricker) and 0.003 (random walk). Both are driven by 2005: with the 2005 residual left out they are 0.26 and 0.98. If a learner asks for a test, say that the QQ plot shows the same thing and also shows which year causes it.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 2 takes about 14 minutes. Learners who restarted R get pitt, dat_pitt, ricker_pitt and walk_pitt back by running upper-pitt-river.R from the top; paste the first four lines of the solution into the shared notes document for anyone whose script is incomplete. Watch for object 'res_long_pitt' not found: the renamed bind_rows() lines must run before the plot. Ask for a green sticky note when the three lag-1 numbers print and row 5 is written. If the class is behind, do the lag-1 numbers and the brood-year plot only, and come back to the QQ plots at the start of Day 2.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 3: if many learners choose (a), say that deleting a year because the model does not like it makes the model seem better than it is in every later check and forecast. This is the end of Day 1. Check with sticky notes that learners have rows 1 to 5 of the Upper Pitt River report card, and collect one-up/one-down feedback. Close with: “Tomorrow: can the model make data like ours, which model do the data support, and do its forecasts work?”


    Checking a Model with Simulation

    Instructor Note

    Open Day 2 by saying what you changed after yesterday’s feedback (5 minutes, not counted in this episode’s time). Then ask everyone to open their project and run the Starting Point chunk (2 minutes): a new R session has no packages and no recipe box. Give learners 5 minutes for the warm-up, alone or in pairs. The line that does not belong is the missing random = mistake from Episode 4. If many learners keep it, run the second chunk of the solution live: all four checks fail.


    Instructor Note

    The 50-refit self-test takes about 2 seconds. Learners do not type self_test(): walk through it line by line while they read it on the page (about 2 minutes), then have them run the summary. Anyone who ran the Starting Point with their own my-recipes.R instead of files/cookbook.R runs source("files/cookbook.R") now, because Challenge 5 uses self_test(). Ask for sticky notes when the self-test table prints.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 4 targets the belief that a higher coverage means better or more precise intervals. If most learners choose (a) or (d), point to the sd_walk panel: 11 estimates sit near zero, far from the truth of 0.13, yet every interval caught it. If many choose (c), say that coverage from 50 refits varies by chance, and that 1.00 is a problem here because of how it arises. If answers are spread out, go back to Harrison’s interval from 0 to Inf in Episode 6. The vote and the discussion take about 3 minutes.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 6 revisits Episode 6, Challenge 4: ask who would now change their answer. Anyone who chose (c) there should now be able to say why it is too strong. If many learners think a zero estimate means the fit failed, go back to Harrison’s four TRUE checks and the AIC difference of 2.


    Comparing Models with AIC

    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when the full table prints, about 40 minutes into the episode. Misconceptions to listen for: “the model with more parameters always wins” (the NPGO model has one more parameter than the Ricker and loses) and “the lowest AIC is the true model” (AIC ranks only the candidates you wrote). If you will skip Episode 10, tell the pooled-NPGO story here in two minutes: across all 19 stocks, NPGO lowers AIC by 16 without shared year effects but raises it by 0.6 with them.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 3 targets misconception M9: if learners accept the colleague’s claim, point at the row counts (64 against 74) and run aic_table() live. Challenge 5 targets M16: if most choose (a), use the change of units in the solution (fish instead of thousands of fish changes model B’s score by 511 and model A’s not at all); if answers are spread out, go back to the first of the four rules. aic_table() cannot catch this mistake when both models keep logRS in their data list, so rule 1 matters. Check with sticky notes that learners have row 7 of the Upper Pitt River report card before the break.


    Many Stocks: Random Effects for Groups

    Instructor Note

    This is the first episode to cut. If you cut it, tell learners where it is, and tell the pooled-NPGO story in two minutes at the end of Episode 9: across all 19 stocks, NPGO lowers AIC by 16 without shared year effects but raises it by 0.6 with them. Every fit here takes under half a second. The optional residual spoiler takes about 3 seconds and the optional profile interval about 5.


    Instructor Note

    If most learners choose (a), point to the shrinkage table when it prints: Quesnel and Bowron have 74 years each and barely move, Gates has 54 years and moves a long way, and Late Shuswap has 74 years but still moves a long way because it is far from the average. If answers are spread out, go back to the bell curve: every stock’s value comes from one distribution, and the pooled model decides how far to trust each stock’s own data.


    Instructor Note

    Ask for sticky notes when the year-effect plot appears. Point out that the year effects in this model are independent from year to year: the decline in the plot comes from the data, not from a random walk.


    Forecasting and Testing Forecasts

    Instructor Note

    Challenge 1 takes about 4 minutes and Challenge 2 about 3. Challenge 1 targets the belief that a confidence interval says where single years fall (first met in Episode 5, where the 95% band held 24% of the Stellako points); if most learners choose (a), show that band plot again and say “the band is about the curve; single years scatter around it by sigma”. Ask two or three learners to read out their sentence on why the prediction interval is wider. Challenge 2 targets “exp() of a log forecast is the mean”; if most choose (a), run the solution code live (median 148, mean 199 thousand). If answers are spread out, go back to the two printed intervals, the 95% confidence interval and the 80% prediction interval, and compare them line by line.


    Instructor Note

    The hindcast takes under 1 second per stock, so it is safe to run live. Ask for sticky notes when the score table prints, and read the four columns aloud with the class before moving on. If score_forecasts() stops with “skill must be size 3 or 1, not 0”, the table has no rows called naive: check the names in bind_rows().


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 3 takes about 3 minutes. If most learners choose (b), point to the score table: the benchmark’s own skill is exactly 1, and every skill is compared with it. If most choose (c), say that coverage above 0.80 means more outcomes inside the intervals than promised. If answers are spread out, go back to the four definitions and read the random walk’s row of the Stellako table together.


    Instructor Note

    Challenge 4 is the longest coding task before the capstone (15 minutes), so have helpers circulate. The hindcast and scoring code is in the handout; learners change the stock and the object names. Learners who finish early can try the optional Challenge 6 at the end of the episode. Watch for the belief that a lower AIC means better forecasts: Upper Pitt River shows a lower AIC without smaller forecast errors, and the capstone share-out returns to it.


    Capstone: A Model Report for a New Stock

    Instructor Note

    The capstone takes 90 minutes: 10 minutes to present the menu, the template and the rubric, 60 minutes of pair work, and 20 minutes of share-out. Form the pairs before you present the template, mixing profiles where you can (an R-confident learner with a domain-confident one). Ask for sticky notes at three checkpoints: after C2 (all checks TRUE), after C7 (the AIC table) and after C8 (the hindcast scores). If pairs fall behind, make rows 5 and 6 optional; never cut rows 2, 3, 7, 8 and 9. If Episode 10 was cut, give the capstone 30 of the 45 minutes saved.


    Instructor Note

    Answer key (values from the filled template; hindcast from 2007; skill = MAE / MAE of the four-year benchmark). Every fit and every refit passed all four checks, and one run of the filled template takes a few seconds.

    Capstone answer key, with the two stocks from class for comparison.

    Chilko 1948-2021, 74 years; spawners 6.6-1182; S_new 257.5 walk 0, BH 0.4, Ricker 1.9: a three-way tie 0.29 to 0.18 0.96 / 0.81 / 1.06 0.53 BH: 1288 (436-3805) AIC 187.22 (best by 2.2), skill 0.89 AIC cannot decide; the hindcast prefers Beverton-Holt; the walk’s intervals are far too narrow

The Ricker random walk finds no drift, but the Beverton-Holt random walk does. Do not report the walk’s 0-to-Inf interval
    Birkenhead 1948-2021, 74 years; spawners 1.6-198, recent years 2.0, 1.6, 23.5; S_new 8.6 walk (8.1 over BH) 0.50 to 0.11 0.93 / 0.85 / 0.90 0.53 walk: 166 (39-698) AIC 220.89 (best by 8.8), skill 0.79 All models only modestly beat the benchmark. The Ricker residuals fail the shape check (QQ). Productivity jumps to 21 recruits per spawner in the last years, when spawners were very few: check those years before trusting the forecast

    (Upper Pitt River) “your turn” stock walk (6.2 over Ricker + NPGO) 0.47 to 0.13 0.78 / 0.78 / 0.82 0.60 walk: 12.4 (4.4-35.2) AIC 182.18 (best by 3.5), skill 0.77 AIC prefers the walk, the hindcast MAE slightly prefers the stationary curves, and NPGO helps

    Further key values:

    • Ricker estimates (alpha in recruits per spawner, S_max in thousand spawners, 95% CI):
      • Quesnel: alpha 9.7 (7.3-13.0), S_max 1046 (468-2338);
      • Late Stuart: 10.2 (7.4-14.1), 527 (194-1435);
      • Chilko: 11.2 (8.4-14.9), 388 (268-560);
      • Harrison: 7.3 (5.3-10.2), 112 (69-179); Beverton-Holt alpha 21.1 (10.1-44.5), S_half 3.7 (1.2-11.4);
      • Birkenhead: 11.4 (7.8-16.5), 77.5 (47.8-125.5).
    • sd_walk: Quesnel 0.22 (0.11-0.43); Late Stuart 0.28 (0.11-0.71); Chilko 0.12 (0.024-0.59); Harrison at zero; Birkenhead 0.48 (0.24-0.94).
    • Simulated-data check, share of random-walk simulations at or above the observed lag-1 correlation of log(R/S): Quesnel 0.375 (observed 0.43); Late Stuart 0.65; Chilko 0.06 (observed 0.46); Harrison 0.235 (Ricker 0.22); Birkenhead 0.78. The Ricker has 0 for every stock except Harrison.
    • Self-test (30 simulations; Harrison tests Beverton-Holt): every refit passes. sd_walk collapses to near zero in 2 of 30 for Quesnel and Late Stuart, 5 for Chilko and 0 for Birkenhead.

    Pairs who pick Harrison will find sd_walk at zero: point them to “Check an SD Near Zero” in Episode 6 and to rule 4 of the AIC rules, and let them choose Beverton-Holt for the self-test and the forecast. Pairs who pick Quesnel should report S_max under the random walk as “beyond the data”, not as a number.


    Instructor Note

    After the share-out, close the workshop outside the counted minutes: minute cards, the post-workshop survey, and one-up/one-down. Point learners to the Going Further page and the Recipe Index, and remind them to keep my-recipes.R, stellako.R, upper-pitt-river.R and the filled template.
